abstract.p: Esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) and gastric cancer (GC) are influenced by genetic and lifestyle factor. We quantified genetic, lifestyle, and joint effect on upper gastrointestinal (UGI) cancer and evaluated the clinical utility of polygenic risk scores (PRS) for risk stratification. We included 5556 participants from a prospective endoscopy-screened cohort in high-risk regions (Linzhou, Cixian, and Feicheng) of China. Parallel genome-wide association studies of ESCC and GC were conducted using baseline and follow-up cases. Cancer type-specific PRSs were applied using developed models in Chinese populations. Information on smoking, alcohol use, body mass index, physical activity, and diet was collected to construct a healthy lifestyle score (HLS). Multivariable logistic and Cox models evaluated associations between PRS, HLS and UGI cancer risk, and risk stratification was assessed by combining PRSs with non-genetic factors. 1050 ESCC and 1015 GC cases were identified, including 203 ESCC and 170 GC incident cases diagnosed during a median follow-up of 5.2 years. A potentially novel GC locus at 6p12.1 (rs72875397) was identified. Higher PRSs were associated with increased risk of ESCC (HR: 1.20; 95% CI: 1.05–1.37) and GC (HR: 1.44; 95% CI: 1.24–1.67). Individuals with high PRS and unfavorable lifestyle had 2.75-fold and 4.18-fold increased risk of ESCC and GC. Adding PRSs to non-genetic models yielded improvements in C-index for ESCC (6.5 %) and GC (7.2%). Gradients of benefit from favorable lifestyle were observed across PRS strata, with substantial reductions in cumulative incidence among individuals at high genetic risk (ESCC: from 14.24% to 5.08%; GC: 13.23% to 4.85%). In summary, PRSs improved risk stratification, and favorable lifestyle reduced UGI cancer risk across genetic strata, especially in those with high PRS, supporting risk-informed personalized prevention.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Esophageal cancer (EC) and gastric cancer (GC) are common upper gastrointestinal (UGI) cancers and rank fifth and seventh worldwide in terms of absolute numbers of deaths according to GLOBOCAN 2022 [1]. Nearly half of UGI cancer cases occur in China, where esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC) accounts for over 90% of EC, and approximately 70% of cardia gastric cancer (CGC) and 50% of non-cardia gastric cancer (NCGC) cases worldwide also occur [2–4]. The symptoms of UGI cancer are generally nonspecific, leading most cases to be diagnosed at advanced stages where prognosis is dismal [5,6]. Therefore, identifying high-risk individuals and determining who may benefit most from targeted prevention are critical steps toward precision prevention of UGI cancers.

Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have identified thousands of variants associated with complex diseases and traits [7]. Polygenic risk scores (PRS) aggregate the effects of multiple risk-associated variants to quantify individuals’ genetic susceptibility [8]. However, GWAS discovery efforts have been disproportionately conducted in populations of European ancestry, and PRSs derived from these datasets often show reduced predictive accuracy in non-European populations, potentially widening health disparities [9]. The heritability of UGI cancer in Chinese population has been estimated at 20% [10]. Although several PRSs for UGI cancer have been developed based on GWAS conducted in Chinese population [11–14], most have been validated in biobank-based datasets. Evidence remains limited regarding the optimization and calibration of PRSs in specific high-risk populations, which may not accurately capture real-world applicability in endoscopy-screened participants from high-risk regions with implemented screening programs. Further research is needed to investigate whether PRSs improve risk prediction and screening effectiveness in high-risk populations that are likely to be targeted for UGI cancer screening. Additionally, some variants confer different risks for GC subsites (cardia vs. non-cardia) [15], yet the performance of PRS constructed for overall GC in predicting subtype-specific disease risk remains unclear.

Infectious and lifestyle factors have also been identified as having important roles in the development of UGI cancer [4]. As the leading risk factor and primary prevention target for GC, Helicobacter pylori eradication has shown variable long-term benefits across genetic susceptibility levels in high-risk regions [16]. This complex interplay between genetic and environmental exposure in cancer carcinogenesis has also been reported in behavioral risk factors [11,12,17]. About 48.5% of EC and 59.8% of GC cases in China were attributed to lifestyle factors, including smoking, alcohol use, and unhealthy diet [18]. The extent to which healthy lifestyle can influence the impact of genetic predisposition on UGI cancer risk in high-risk Chinese populations remains uncertain, particularly given potential regional variations in genetic structure and environmental exposures [19,20].

We conducted a prospective cohort study among participants in an endoscopic screening program in UGI cancer high-risk regions of China. Our primary aims were to investigate associations between PRSs and the risk of ESCC and GC and further assess the predictive and clinical utility of PRSs, as well as to evaluate whether benefits in terms of absolute risk reductions from adherence to healthy lifestyle differ across PRS strata. Secondary aims were to identify novel genetic loci and evaluate previously reported single nucleotide variants (SNVs), to enhance the understanding of genetic susceptibility among high-risk populations of UGI cancers.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: Participants were recruited from a UGI cancer screening program between 2015 and 2022 in high-risk regions of China (Supplementary Methods and Fig. S1 online). Details of the program have been described previously [21]. Briefly, the program targeted permanent residents aged ≥ 40 years in selected centers covering entire counties or cities. All enrolled participants underwent endoscopic screening, completed a standardized questionnaire (including demographic, socioeconomic and lifestyle factors), and provided biological samples. Prevalent ESCC and GC cases were defined as those diagnosed at baseline, while incident cases were newly obtained among participants with normal baseline endoscopy during follow-up through Sep 1, 2024, the latest available surveillance data. Further details on case definition and classification criteria are described in the Supplementary Methods (online). All participants provided written informed consent in accordance with the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki guidelines, and the study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the Cancer Hospital, Chinese Academy of Medical Sciences (Approval number: 22/324–3526).

sec.title: Genotyping and imputation
sec.p: Genotyping was performed on blood DNA using the Asian Screening Array (Illumina, San Diego, USA). After standard quality control, genotype imputation was performed using the CHN100K Imputation Server with a reference panel constructed from 25,734 Chinese individuals [22]. Imputation quality thresholds (INFO > 0.3) were applied to retain imputed variants for validation. The final dataset retained over 4 million SNVs, including the 530,000 genotyped SNVs originally submitted for imputation. Quality control parameters are outlined in Table S1 (online).

sec.title: GWAS and functional annotation
sec.p: GWAS of ESCC and GC were performed using REGENIE, a machine-learning method [23]. In Step 1 of the REGENIE framework, cross-validated ridge regression was applied to blocks of array-genotyped SNVs to generate polygenic predictors accounting for local linkage disequilibrium (LD). In Step 2, association testing for binary traits was performed using fast Firth logistic regression, incorporating the Step 1 leave-one-chromosome-out predictions as a covariate. Age, sex, site and the first five principal components (PCs) were included as covariates to account for potential confounding effects and population stratification. Subsequently, GWAS summary statistics from our study and an independent NCI-GWAS (see Supplementary Methods online for details) were meta-analyzed in METAL using the inverse variance-weighted fixed-effects model to assess the robustness of genome-wide significant findings. Regional mapping and functional annotation were performed using LocusZoom [24] and FUMA v1.7.0 [25] for variants identified with P < 5×10−8 in our GWAS or the meta-GWAS. Differential expression patterns of associated genes were compared using TCGA and GTEx databases (see Supplementary Methods online for details). Data visualization was generated using the R packages CMplot and ggplot2 (R v.4.2.1).

sec.title: Selection of PRS
sec.p: Given the limited genome-wide significant signals in our GWAS, we compared several PRS models previously developed in Chinese populations and selected those with larger discovery GWAS sample sizes and better predictive performance for subsequent analyses [11,12,16,26]. Specifically, PRS 25 for ESCC and PRS 112 for GC were finally adopted based on their superior discrimination compared with alternative models (Fig. S2 online). Details of selected SNVs are provided in Table S2–4 (online). To increase statistical power, we meta-analyzed risk estimates comparing the highest and lowest PRS quantiles between our data and original studies [11,12]. In the GC subgroup, the same PRS model was applied to both CGC and NCGC. Participants were categorized into low (Q1), intermediate (Q2–Q3), and high (Q4) genetic risk groups according to PRS quartiles based on the distribution among healthy individuals. PRS selection and calculation are described in the Supplementary Methods (online).

sec.title: Healthy lifestyle score
sec.p: Five modifiable lifestyle factors defining a healthy lifestyle were included, based on recommendations from World Cancer Research Fund/American Institute of Cancer Research, Dietary Guidelines for Chinese Residents, and previous studies [27–30]: smoking, alcohol use, body mass index (BMI), physical activity and dietary habits. Each variable was scored as 0 or 1 based on predefined criteria for healthy behavior (see Table S5 online for definitions and scoring criteria). For dietary habits, a simplified dietary score was constructed from the intake frequency of six food items (fresh vegetables, fresh fruits, whole grains, red and processed meat, pickled foods, and hot foods). The unweighted healthy lifestyle score (HLS), ranging from 0 to 5, was calculated by summing scores of five factors. Participants were categorized into three lifestyle groups: unfavorable (HLS: 0–1), intermediate (2–3), and favorable (4–5). Given the known heterogeneity in risk factor effects, the weighted HLS was derived based on the β coefficients for each lifestyle factor from Cox proportional hazards models that included all lifestyle variables, adjusted for age, sex, site, education, income, digestive disease history, and family history of UGI cancer, and the first five PCs (Table S6 online). The weighted score was further categorized into favorable, intermediate, and unfavorable according to the distribution of the unweighted HLS.

sec.title: Covariate definition
sec.p: Other covariates were obtained through a baseline questionnaire, including age, sex, site, education level, income level, digestive disease history, and family history of UGI cancers. Site referred to the screening location, including Linzhou, Cixian and Feicheng. Education level was categorized as middle school or above versus illiterate or primary school. Income level was dichotomized using an annual threshold of 30,000 CNY. Digestive disease history was defined as a self-reported previous diagnosis of reflux esophagitis, chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, or gastrointestinal polyps. All covariates were missing < 8% (see Table S7 online for covariate description and missingness).

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Demographic characteristics were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD), median with interquartile range (IQR) or frequencies with percentages. Given the complexity of real-world screening programs, where cases may be detected either at baseline or during follow-up, we employed a dual analytical strategy to enhance statistical power. Multivariable logistic models were used to preliminarily assess overall association between PRS (quartiles and per SD increase) and ESCC and GC (overall and by anatomical subsite) at baseline or during follow-up. Cox proportional hazards models with follow-up time as the time scale were applied to estimate time-to-event risk among participants free of UGI cancer at baseline. Schoenfeld residuals indicated no violation of the proportional hazard assumption. Follow-up time was defined as the time from baseline screening to the date of UGI cancer diagnosis, loss to follow-up or death, whichever occurred first. The association between HLS and UGI cancer risk was evaluated using the same dual approach as for PRS. Multiplicative interactions between PRS and HLS were assessed using the Wald test by adding an interaction term to the Cox models. Additive interactions were estimated by calculating the relative excess risk due to interaction (RERI) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). All models were adjusted for age, sex, site, education, income, digestive disease history, family history and the first five PCs to account for potential confounding. PRS and HLS were mutually adjusted. Missing covariates were handled using multiple imputation with the R package mice. C-statistics for survival data were used to estimate the improvement in discrimination after adding the PRSs to base models comprising HLS and demographic factors. Differences in C-statistics between models and 95% CIs were assessed using a bootstrap procedure with 1000 replications. Net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) were further applied to examine the improvement of the baseline traditional risk model after adding PRS, with cut-offs defined by quartiles of UGI cancer risk. The incidence rates of ESCC and GC among the different genetic risk groups were shown with Kaplan-Meier curves, and the absolute risk reduction (ARR) was defined as the difference in 5-year cumulative incidence between unfavorable and favorable lifestyle groups. Weighted least-squares models were used to evaluate the trend in ARR across genetic risk groups. Risk advancement period (RAP) representing the baseline age difference at which individuals with different genetic risks reached the same risk of UGI cancer was calculated according to Brenner et al. [31].

To assess the robustness of our results, we conducted sensitivity analyses as follows: (1) repeated analyses after excluding participants with missing covariate data; (2) examined the associations between PRS, weighted HLS and UGI cancer risk; (3) repeated analyses after excluding participants who were diagnosed with UGI cancer within the first year of follow-up; (4) performed competing risk analysis using Fine-Gray models, treating deaths during follow-up as the competing event [32]; and (5) applied the sex and age stratification analysis.

All statistical tests were two-sided, and P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant, except for GWAS where a genome-wide significance threshold was applied as described above. Statistical analyses were conducted using R software (version 4.4.2), PLINK (version 1.9), and REGENIE (version 4.1).

sec.title: Baseline characteristics of study population
sec.p: A total of 5556 participants were included in this study. Baseline characteristics are presented in Table 1 and Table S8 (online). The median age was 62 years, and 3176 of the participants (57.16%) were male. Most participants had an intermediate (63.98%) HLS, including two or three healthy lifestyle factors. Overall, 2013 UGI cancers were identified at baseline or during follow-up, including 1050 ESCC and 1015 GC cases. Among these, 203 incident ESCC and 170 incident GC cases were diagnosed during a median follow-up of 5.2 years. Compared with participants without UGI cancer, individuals with ESCC or GC had higher disease-specific PRS (ESCC: 2.15 vs 1.94; GC: −0.47 vs −0.73) and were more likely to have an unfavorable lifestyle, digestive disease history and family history of UGI cancers, and lower educational and income level. Distributions of specific lifestyle factors are presented in Table S9–10 (online).

sec.title: GWAS and meta-analysis of ESCC and GC in high-risk screening populations and functional analysis with bioinformatics
sec.p: We identified a significant locus at 10q23.3, comprising 34 candidate SNVs in high LD (r2 > 0.6) that exhibited comparable genome-wide significant P-values through GWAS of ESCC (Fig. 1). The quantile-quantile plot indicated no evidence of genomic inflation (λ = 1.047). The lead SNV (rs12263737) was in strong LD (r2 = 0.989) with rs2274223, a previously reported variant significantly associated with ESCC (Table S11, Fig. S3 online). The meta-GWAS confirmed genome-wide significance at 10q23.3, 2q33.1, and 22q12.1, and further identified an additional locus at 2q11.1, which was close to the suggestive threshold in each dataset (Table S12 online). Additionally, 13 SNVs from GWAS Catalog-reported significant loci were associated with ESCC risk at P < 0.05 in the high-risk population (Table S13 online). Similarly, the GWAS of GC identified the same locus at 10q23.3, with lead SNV (rs10882416) and 85 additional SNVs in high LD, as well as a potentially novel locus at 6p12.1 (lead SNV rs72875397) (Table S11, Fig. S3 online). The quantile-quantile plot showed no evidence of inflation (λ = 1.048) (Fig. 1). In the meta-GWAS, these two loci remained genome-wide significant, along with previously reported loci at 1q22, 5p13.1 (Table S12 online). In addition, 18 previously reported SNVs were associated with GC risk (Table S14 online). Most candidate SNVs for ESCC and GC were located in intronic regions (Fig. S4 online).

Gene-based GWAS was conducted by mapping SNVs to protein-coding genes, and both PLCE1 and NOC3L showed significant associations with ESCC and GC after Bonferroni correction (Fig. S5 online). Lead SNVs at the NOC3L locus (ESCC: rs12263737; GC: rs10882416) were identified as cis-eQTLs in muscularis layers of multiple gastrointestinal tissues (Table S15 online). Additionally, NOC3L was overexpressed in both ESCC and GC versus adjacent or independent normal tissues, while PLCE1 exhibited lower expression in ESCC and GC tissues (Fig. S6 online).

sec.title: Association between PRS and prevalent and incident UGI cancers
sec.p: Fig. 2 shows clear divergence in score distribution between cases and participants without UGI cancers, with case proportions increasing consistently across PRS quartiles. In the GC subgroup, the difference in PRS between CGC cases and participants without CGC was more pronounced than that for NCGC cases (Fig. S7 online).

The multivariable logistic model showed significant associations between PRS and prevalent ESCC and GC in high-risk regions for UGI cancer (Table 2). Each 1 SD increase in PRS was associated with adjusted odds ratios (ORs) of 1.26 (95% CI: 1.17–1.36) for ESCC and 1.35 (95% CI: 1.25–1.45) for GC. In the fully adjusted model with PRS as quantiles, participants in the highest quartile of the disease-specific PRS had a 1.82-fold increased risk of ESCC (95% CI: 1.47–2.25) and a 2.14-fold increased risk of GC (95% CI: 1.74–2.64) compared to those in the lowest quartile. In GC subtype analysis, the highest PRS quartile was associated with a 2.29-fold increased risk of CGC (95% CI: 1.81–2.91) and 2.02-fold for NCGC (95% CI: 1.48–2.78) (Table S16 online).

In the prospective analysis among the subset of 3906 participants free of UGI cancers at baseline, higher PRSs were also associated with increased risk of ESCC and GC, both as continuous variables and by quantiles. Specifically, the adjusted hazard ratios (HRs) per 1 SD increase were 1.20 (95% CI: 1.05–1.37) for ESCC and 1.44 (95% CI: 1.24–1.67) for GC, consistent with cross-sectional estimates. Compared with individuals in the lowest PRS quartile, those in the highest had a 1.70-fold increased risk of ESCC (95% CI: 1.14–2.54) and 2.35-fold increased risk of GC (95% CI: 1.52–3.64) (Table 2). In GC subtype analysis, the HRs per 1 SD increase were 1.51 (95% CI: 1.26–1.80) for CGC and 1.37 for NCGC (95% CI: 1.09–1.72) (Table S16 online).

We further meta-analyzed risk estimates by comparing the highest versus lowest categories of disease-specific PRS from our prospective study with those reported in the original studies. The pooled associations for ESCC (highest vs. lowest = 2.35; 95% CI: 1.44–3.82) and GC (highest vs. lowest = 1.92; 95% CI: 1.57–2.34) were similar to our findings (Fig. S8 online). Furthermore, cumulative incidence curves for ESCC and GC by genetic risk group demonstrated that higher genetic risk was associated with increased risk of ESCC (log-rank P = 0.04) and GC (log-rank P < 0.001) (Fig. S9 online). Compared with individuals at high genetic risk, those with low genetic risk had RAPs of −11.7 years for ESCC and −13.1 years for GC (Table S17 online). In GC subtypes, this association was more pronounced for CGC (P < 0.001) than NCGC (P = 0.009) (Fig. S10 online).

sec.title: Association between HLS and prevalent and incident UGI cancers
sec.p: As shown in Table S18 (online), individuals with an unfavorable HLS had higher risks of prevalent ESCC (OR: 2.01; 95% CI: 1.50–2.68) and GC (OR: 1.88; 95% CI: 1.42–2.50) compared to those with a favorable HLS. In multivariable logistic models, smoking and unfavorable BMI were significantly associated with prevalent ESCC and GC. Positive but not significant associations with ESCC or GC were observed for eight of the remaining unfavorable lifestyle factors, potentially due to limited statistical power (Table S19 online). Similar associations of HLS with incident ESCC (HR: 1.78; 95% CI: 1.04–3.03) and GC (HR: 1.81; 95% CI: 1.02–3.20) were observed among participants free of UGI cancers at baseline (Table S18, 20 online).

sec.title: Combined genetic and lifestyle effects on future UGI cancer risk
sec.p: Fig. 3 illustrates association between lifestyle and incident ESCC and GC stratified by genetic risk. We found a joint association of higher genetic risk and unfavorable lifestyle with increased risk of incident ESCC and GC. Compared with participants with low genetic risk and favorable lifestyle, those with both high genetic risk and unfavorable lifestyle had substantially increased risks of ESCC (HR: 2.75; 95% CI: 1.00–7.57) and GC (HR: 4.18; 95% CI: 1.55–11.25). No evidence of additive or multiplicative interactions was observed (Table S21, 22 online). Adding the PRSs to the baseline model including age, sex and HLS significantly improved risk discrimination for incident ESCC (C-statistic change: 6.5%, P = 0.001) and GC (change: 7.2%, P = 0.001) (Table S23 online). Consistently, adding the PRSs significantly improved risk reclassification, with 25.6% of participants reclassified for ESCC and 29.8% for GC. The IDI values supported this improvement (0.011 for ESCC, and 0.013 for GC) (Table S24 online). We then assessed the extent to which the elevated risk associated with high genetic predisposition could be offset by favorable lifestyle. A substantial reduction in the absolute risk of incident ESCC (ARR: 9.16%) and GC (ARR: 8.38%) was observed among individuals adhering to a favorable lifestyle in high genetic risk group when those with favorable lifestyle were used as the reference groups (Fig. 3). Each combination of lifestyle factors and genetic risk was associated with the risk of ESCC and GC (Fig. S11 online). Regarding ARRs, a significant gradient of dietary benefit was observed across genetic risk groups for ESCC (P = 0.01) (Fig. S12 online).

sec.title: Sensitivity analyses
sec.p: Similar association patterns were observed across sensitivity analyses. The association of PRS, unweighted and weighted HLS, and their combined effect with UGI cancer risk remained essentially unchanged after excluding participants with missing covariate data or those diagnosed within the first-year follow-up, as well as when using Fine-Gray models to account for competing risk events (Fig. S13–15, Table S25–32 online). When stratified by sex and age, the association between PRS and UGI cancer risk was slightly stronger among males and was more pronounced in participants aged ⩽60 years. The protective association of a healthy lifestyle was consistent across age strata. No significant interactions were observed between sex or age and PRS or HLS (Table S33,34 online).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In the study of high-risk regions for UGI cancers, we validated that two PRSs developed in the general population could effectively stratify UGI cancer risk in the endoscopically screened population from these high-risk areas. Genetic risk and unfavorable lifestyle independently contributed to UGI cancer risk, while adherence to a healthy lifestyle reduced risk across all genetic risk levels, with substantial gradients in benefit. Furthermore, we conducted parallel GWASs for ESCC and GC, replicated the previously reported susceptibility locus at 10q23.3, and identified a potentially novel locus at 6p12.1 for GC supported by replication and meta-GWAS.

PRS has been shown to quantify genetic susceptibility at the population level. PRSs developed using GWAS conducted in Chinese population have demonstrated risk stratification in prior studies. We independently validated the published PRS 25 of ESCC and PRS 112 of GC in our screening cohort from high-risk regions and observed a significant increase in UGI cancer risk among individuals with higher PRSs [11,12]. The observed differences in PRS effects between ESCC and GC may partly reflect differences in their underlying genetic architecture, as well as variations in PRS construction strategies across studies. Although previous GWAS included a small proportion of cases from high-risk regions for UGI cancers (15.8% for GC and 13.9% for ESCC), most were based on general populations or biobank-based datasets, which may limit their representativeness for real-world high-risk populations. Compared with the source population used for PRS development, our screening cohort also showed a male predominance and had an older age distribution, which is associated with higher risk of UGI cancers [33]. Although the definitions of risk factors differed across studies, both cases and controls in our study exhibited lower percentages of smokers and drinkers than the source population. Similar patterns were observed among high-risk subgroups within the source population. These discrepancies likely reflect differences in environmental exposures between general and high-risk populations. In addition, several studies have reported geographic variation in the incidence of UGI cancers and pronounced familial aggregation in high-risk regions, suggesting differences in population-specific genetic backgrounds [34,35]. These differences were not fully captured in biobank-based general population datasets, which may introduce selection bias. Methodological heterogeneity in PRS construction may further influence transferability across populations [7]. These distinctions underscore the importance of evaluating PRS performance in representative screening populations, which is essential for assessing the practical utility in early detection strategies and endoscopic resource allocation. Notably, the proportion of ESCC and GC cases increased steadily across PRS quartiles, and the meta-analysis of our current and previous studies confirmed that higher disease-specific PRSs were associated with increased ESCC and GC risk, respectively. This provided potential evidence of PRS in calibrating risk prediction models in endoscopically screened population of high-risk regions [36]. RAP analysis suggested that compared with individuals at high genetic risk, those at low genetic risk reached equivalent ESCC and GC risk levels approximately 11.7 and 13.1 years later, respectively. Similarly, a large lung cancer modeling study reported that the age at which individuals crossed recommended screening threshold varied by 4–8 years across PRS strata [37]. These findings suggested that individual’s PRS could be informative regarding optimal age for screening initiation. A cost-effectiveness modeling study in China further demonstrated that PRS-based stratified screening could avoid more UGI cancer deaths and save more quality-adjusted life-years [38]. Nevertheless, genotyping costs and the modest incremental prediction from PRSs remained practical constraints, which underscored the need to incorporate other risk factors and optimize screening resources. Additionally, the association between PRS and GC risk appeared stronger in CGC than in NCGC, as evidenced by more pronounced differences in PRS distributions compared with shared controls. One possible explanation is the population structure of the training dataset used for PRS construction. The PRS applied in our study was developed from a meta-GWAS combining multiple cohorts, in which 42% of GC cases with defined subsites were CGC from high-risk regions similar to our cohort, whereas most NCGC were from different geographic regions [12]. The PRS may more effectively capture genetic susceptibility in CGC due to greater similarity in genetic architecture and environmental background. This finding aligned with previous comparative GWAS of GC subtypes in Asian populations and underscored the need to further develop subtype-specific PRSs to improve precision prevention [39].

Several previous studies have explored the interaction between PRS and modifiable risk factors on UGI cancer risk, most of which reported similar effects of modifiable factors across different levels of genetic susceptibility. A previous study of European population reported that individuals at high genetic risk could reduce UGI cancer risk by adhering to a healthy dietary pattern [17]. Similarly, another study developing a PRS for GC demonstrated a combined effect of genetic risk and lifestyle factors consisting of smoking, alcohol use, pickled foods, vegetables and fruits [12]. However, as many lifestyle factors such as unhealthy BMI, red and processed meat and physical activity were also associated with UGI cancer risk and were correlated, estimating the joint effect of a single factor with PRS would be inaccurate [18,20]. Therefore, our study provided a more comprehensive assessment of genetic risk, lifestyle factors and their combined effect on UGI cancer risk. We found that individuals with high polygenic risk and unfavorable lifestyle had nearly 3 to 4-fold increased risk compared to those with low polygenic risk and favorable lifestyle. The clinical utility of PRS in UGI cancer risk stratification remained uncertain when combined with traditional risk factors. Only one study reported an increase of 0.058 in C-index after adding the PRS of ESCC to a clinical model [11]. We also observed statistically significant yet modest improvements in discrimination of the PRS over a baseline model in our cohort recruited from a real-world UGI cancer screening program. Although the C-statistics for these PRSs were relatively modest, slight improvements in discrimination can translate into meaningful population benefits, such as higher detection rates and fewer endoscopies per case detected, in the context of large-scale screening programs [40–42]. It is encouraging that adherence to a favorable lifestyle could nearly offset the cumulative risk conferred by high genetic predisposition, with a significant gradient of benefits across genetic risk categories. These findings support personalized lifestyle recommendations tailored to genetic background, which may be particularly impactful in settings where the proportions of healthy behaviors remain suboptimal in China [43]. Specifically, healthy dietary pattern was associated with a significantly greater ARR for ESCC across increasing genetic risk levels. Recent MR studies in East Asian populations further supported our observed findings by confirming the causal relationship between unhealthy lifestyle factors and elevated UGI cancer risk. In particular, genetically predicted smoking was causally associated with esophageal cancer, whereas the association between BMI and GC risk exhibited a U-shaped association [44,45], which underscored the importance of lifestyle interventions in primary prevention. In addition, previous studies have shown for cancers strongly driven by a dominant environmental exposure (such as H. pylori in GC), the marginal contribution of genetic variants to risk prediction may be limited [46]. Emerging evidence integrating genetic susceptibility with transcriptomic information suggested greater benefits of H. pylori treatment in individuals at higher genetic risk [47]. These findings highlighted the need to integrate genetic, infectious and modifiable behavioral factors to enable more targeted precision prevention strategies in high-risk populations [48].

A parallel GWAS previously conducted in a Chinese population identified 10q23.3 as a shared susceptibility locus for UGI cancers, which was replicated in our study. These reported variants were located within a regulatory region flanked by two recombination hotspots, including PLCE1 and NOC3L. Fine-mapping and gene-level analysis in our study further supported these results [49]. PLCE1, a unique member of the phospholipase C family, promotes progression of ESCC by regulating the replicative helicase MCM7 through multiple pathways [50]. NOC3L, which encodes a DNA replication regulator, has been speculated to contribute to GC development by enhancing systemic inflammation and promoting adipogenesis [51]. Complementary evidence from gene expression analysis supported the biological relevance of these genes, with PLCE1 shown to be downregulated in ESCC and GC tissue, while NOC3L was upregulated in tumors compared to adjacent or independent normal tissues. Furthermore, cis-eQTL analysis of gastrointestinal tissues indicated that lead SNVs (rs12263737 for ESCC and rs10882416 for GC) may directly regulate NOC3L expression. The association between rs72875397 at 6p12.1 and GC risk also reached genome-wide significance, which was supported by subsequent meta-GWAS. This variant lay in an intergenic region near PRIM2, a gene that may be implicated in tumorigenesis by promoting DNA replication and mismatch repair [52,53]. While the association appears promising, limited functional evidence supporting regulatory effects underscored the need for further studies to clarify underlying mechanisms. These findings expanded our understanding of genetic basis of UGI cancer risk and provided evidence for gene-specific roles in its development. However, our study had over 95% power to detect variants with moderate effects (OR > 1.5), but less than 20% power for small-effect variants (OR < 1.3) due to the sample size, which may partly explain the lack of additional genome-wide significant loci.

The strengths of our study included the use of the prospective screening cohort with well-defined phenotypes and high-quality outcomes, which enabled rigorous evaluation of genetic risk in the context of comprehensive lifestyle factors. Additionally, we conducted parallel GWAS to identify susceptibility loci for ESCC and GC. However, several limitations should be noted. First, lifestyle and covariate information were self-reported at baseline and longitudinal changes were not captured. Possible measurement and classification errors may have biased associations toward the null. Second, although analyses were adjusted for known confounders, our results may be influenced by unmeasured confounding, particularly from important risk factors such as H. pylori infection. Third, stratification by both genetic risk and lifestyle factor resulted in relatively small sample sizes in certain subgroups, leading to wide CIs around point estimates. Further validation in independent populations is warranted. Fourth, the construction of prediction models without the independent validation set may limit the assessment of the accuracy of PRS-enhanced risk prediction, and further validation is needed in additional datasets representing different populations and settings. Finally, our study was limited to Han Chinese participants. Only one published full-scale GWAS of ESCC in a non-Han population has been reported and the results differed dramatically from the work in East Asia [54]. In contrast, preliminary work in GC suggests genetic risk may be similar across different racial backgrounds [14].

In conclusion, our study identified a potentially novel locus for GC and demonstrated the PRS could improve UGI cancer prediction and risk stratification in endoscopically screened populations from high-risk regions. Adherence to a healthy lifestyle was associated with reduced UGI cancer risk across all levels of genetic susceptibility, with the greatest benefit observed among individuals at high genetic risk. These findings provided evidence to support the development of personalized lifestyle recommendations tailored to the individual’s genetic risk and highlighted the potential value of incorporating genetic information into stratified prevention strategies for UGI cancers.
